;;; private/org-workflow/config.el -*- lexical-binding: t; -*-

;; Org-mode workflow configuration including:
;; - Basic org settings
;; - org-super-agenda custom views
;; - org-roam capture templates and project management
;; - org-download WSL integration

;; org setup
(setq org-directory "~/org/")
(after! org
  (setq org-startup-indented t
        org-indent-mode t
        org-startup-folded t))

(use-package! org-super-agenda
  :after org-agenda
  :init
  (setq org-agenda-skip-scheduled-if-done t
        org-agenda-skip-deadline-if-done t
        org-agenda-include-deadlines t
        org-agenda-block-separator nil
        org-agenda-compact-blocks t
        org-agenda-start-day nil ;; i.e. today
        org-agenda-start-on-weekday nil)
  (setq org-agenda-custom-commands
        '(("c" "Super view"
           ((agenda "" ((org-agenda-overriding-header "")
                        (org-super-agenda-groups
                         '((:name "Today"
                            :time-grid t
                            :date today
                            :order 1)))))
            (alltodo "" ((org-agenda-overriding-header "")
                         (org-super-agenda-groups
                          '((:log t)
                            (:name "To refile"
                             :file-path "refile\\.org")
                            (:name "Next to do"
                             :todo "NEXT"
                             :order 1)
                            (:name "Important"
                             :priority "A"
                             :order 6)
                            (:name "Today's tasks"
                             :file-path  "journals/")
                            (:name "Due Today"
                             :deadline today
                             :order 2)
                            (:name "Scheduled Soon"
                             :deadline future
                             :order 8)
                            (:name "Overdue"
                             :deadline past
                             :order 7)
                            (:name "Meetings"
                             :and (:todo "MEET" :scheduled future)
                             :order 10)
                            (:discard (:not (:todo "TODO")))))))))))
  :config
  (org-super-agenda-mode))

;; Org Roam
(after! org-roam
  (setq org-roam-dailies-directory "journals/"
        rmh-elfeed-org-files '("~/org/roam/pages/news_feeds.org")
        org-roam-capture-templates
        '(("d" "default" plain
           "%?" :target
           (file+head "pages/${slug}.org" "#+title: ${title}\n")
           :unnarrowed t)
          ;; TODO look at how filetags work
          ;; https://d12frosted.io/posts/2020-06-25-task-management-with-roam-vol3.html
          ("c" "Add a new contact")
          ("cc" "Normal contact" plain
           "One date stamped heading for last contact %?" :target
           (file+head "pages/contacts/${slug}.org" "#+title: ${title}\n")
           :unnarrowed t)
          ("co" "o11n contact" plain
           "\nOne date stamped heading for last contact\n %?" :target
           (file+head "pages/contacts/${slug}.org" "#+title: ${title}\n#+filetags: o11n\n")
           :unnarrowed t)
          ;; TODO add an agenda specific capture?
          ;; https://systemcrafters.net/build-a-second-brain-in-emacs/capturing-notes-efficiently/
          ("p" "Project specific notes capture")
          ("pp" "o11n projects - primary" plain
           "%?" :target
           (file+head "projects/o11n-${slug}.org" "#+title: ${title}\n#+filetags: project:o11n\n")
           :unnarrowed t)
          ("pm" "MEPS projects" plain
           "%?" :target
           (file+head "projects/meps-${slug}.org" "#+title: ${title}\n#+filetags: project:meps\n")
           :unnarrowed t)
          ("pv" "AVS projects" plain
           "%?" :target
           (file+head "projects/avs-${slug}.org" "#+title: ${title}\n#+filetags: project:avs\n")
           :unnarrowed t)
          ("pa" "Apps projects" plain
           "%?" :target
           (file+head "projects/apps-${slug}.org" "#+title: ${title}\n#+filetags: project:apps\n")
           :unnarrowed t)))

  ;; https://github.com/org-roam/org-roam/wiki/User-contributed-Tricks#showing-node-hierarchy
  (cl-defmethod org-roam-node-hierarchy ((node org-roam-node))
    (let ((level (org-roam-node-level node)))
      (concat
       (when (> level 0) (concat (org-roam-node-file-title node) " > "))
       (when (> level 1) (concat (string-join (org-roam-node-olp node) " > ") " > "))
       (org-roam-node-title node))))
  ;; (setq org-roam-node-display-template "${hierarchy:*} ${tags:20}")

  (defun sme/org-roam-filter-by-tag (tag-name)
    "Return a filter function that checks if a node has TAG-NAME."
    (lambda (node)
      (member tag-name (org-roam-node-tags node))))

  ;; Taken from https://systemcrafters.net/build-a-second-brain-in-emacs/5-org-roam-hacks/
  ;; trying it mostly as default for now
  (defun sme/org-roam-o11n-finalize-hook ()
    "Adds the captured project file to `org-agenda-files' if the
capture was not aborted."
    ;; Remove the hook since it was added temporarily
    (remove-hook 'org-capture-after-finalize-hook #'sme/org-roam-o11n-finalize-hook)

    ;; Add o11n file to the agenda list if the capture was confirmed
    (unless org-note-abort
      (with-current-buffer (org-capture-get :buffer)
        (add-to-list 'org-agenda-files (buffer-file-name)))))

  (defun sme/org-roam-find-project ()
    (interactive)
    ;; Add the project file to the agenda after capture is finished
    (add-hook 'org-capture-after-finalize-hook #'sme/org-roam-o11n-finalize-hook)

    ;; Select a project file to open, creating it if necessary
    (org-roam-node-find
     nil
     nil
     (sme/org-roam-filter-by-tag "o11n")
     :templates
     '(("p" "project" plain "* Goals\n\n%?\n\n* Tasks\n\n** TODO Add initial tasks\n\n* Dates\n\n"
        :if-new (file+head "projects/%<%Y%m%d%H%M%S>-o11n-${slug}.org" "#+title: ${title}\n#+category: ${title}\n#+filetags: project:o11n\n")
        :unnarrowed t))))

  ;; after org-roam ends here
  )

content.text:
I designed this without changing anything. It's one swamp model that takes Org or Markdown, builds a reveal.js deck with the right engine, and stores the HTML as a versioned file artifact in swamp data. Your existing `SPC o s` swamp entry in Emacs would drive it.

## What's already in place

- **Doom:** `(org +dragndrop +present +pretty +roam)` in `config/doom/init.el`. `+present` installs **org-re-reveal 3.39.0**, **htmlize** and **reveal.js 6.0.1**. They are already built under `~/.config/emacs/.local/straight/build-31.1/`.
- **You don't set any reveal options.** Nothing in your config sets `org-re-reveal-root`, so it falls back to `"./reveal.js"`. Today's exports only work if a reveal.js checkout sits next to the `.org` file.
- **Nix packages:** `pandoc` 3.7 and `chromium` (in `home/sme/shared/packages.nix`), plus Emacs 31.1.
- **Emacs integration:** the `private/swamp` module loads `webframp/emacs-swamp` and maps `swamp-dispatch` to `SPC o s`.
- **Storing files in swamp:** `redmine/extensions/models/redmine/redmine.ts:985` shows the pattern. It declares a `files:` spec and writes bytes with `context.createFileWriter(spec, name, { contentType }).writeAll(bytes)`.

## The extension: `@webframp/presentation`

There is one model type, `@webframp/presentation/deck`. It follows the repo's CLI-wrapping pattern (`Deno.Command`, tested with `withMockedCommand`).

**Global args:**

| arg | default | purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `revealVersion` | `"5.2.1"` | One constant feeds the CDN URL, the provenance record and the pandoc `-V revealjs-url`, so the version is set in one place. |
| `revealRoot` | `cdn` | `cdn` loads reveal.js from jsdelivr at that version. `local:<path>` points at a checkout, e.g. Doom's straight repo, for offline or single-file builds. |
| `emacs` | `"emacs"` | Path to the Emacs binary. |
| `orgLoadPath` | auto-discovered | Finds the `straight/build-<ver>/{org,org-re-reveal,htmlize}` dirs. |
| `theme` | `"black"` | Default theme. Source-file keywords override it. |

**Methods:**

1. **`build`** takes `source` (a path) or `content` (inline text), plus `format` (`auto|org|markdown`), `engine` (`auto|org-re-reveal|pandoc|reveal-markdown`) and `selfContained`.
   - **Org with `org-re-reveal` (the default for `.org`):** runs `emacs --batch -Q`. It loads only the three straight build dirs, not all of Doom, so builds are fast and the same every time. It binds `org-re-reveal-root` and, when `selfContained` is set, `org-re-reveal-single-file`, then calls `org-re-reveal-export-to-html`. All your `#+REVEAL_THEME`, `#+REVEAL_PLUGINS`, `#+ATTR_REVEAL` and `:reveal_background:` markup keeps working. The output matches what `C-c C-e v v` produces in Doom.
   - **Org with `pandoc` (fallback when Emacs isn't available, e.g. CI):** runs `pandoc -f org -t revealjs`. It ignores `#+REVEAL_*` keywords and records a warning in the resource.
   - **Markdown with `pandoc` (the default for `.md`):** runs `pandoc -t revealjs -s`. Headings set the slide level, `---` breaks slides, `::: notes` holds speaker notes, and `--embed-resources` produces a single file.
   - **Markdown with `reveal-markdown`:** needs no tools at all. The deck uses reveal's own markdown plugin and wraps the source in `<section data-markdown><textarea data-template>`. Rendering happens in the browser, using reveal's `---`/`--`/`Note:` separators.
2. **`outline`** parses the source only and does no rendering. It writes slide titles, vertical/horizontal structure, speaker-note word counts and images that are referenced but missing. It's cheap enough to run on every save.
3. **`export_pdf`** (optional) runs chromium headless against `?print-pdf` and writes a `pdf` file artifact.

**Data written per deck**, keyed by a slug of `#+TITLE` or the first `# ` heading, then the filename. No timestamps, so repeated builds version the same name:

- **resource `deck-<slug>`:** source sha256, format, engine, reveal version and root, theme, slide count, titles, warnings, self-contained flag and build duration.
- **file `deck-<slug>`:** `text/html`, the presentation itself.
- **file `deck-<slug>-pdf`:** written only by `export_pdf`.

**Skipping unchanged builds:** if the source hash and build options match the latest `deck-<slug>` resource, `build` records "unchanged" and doesn't write a new file version.

**Workflow and report:**
- **`@webframp/presentation-build`** runs `outline` → `build` → (`export_pdf` when `pdf: true`).
- **`deck-summary`** is a report scoped to the method. It lists slide titles and notes coverage, flags slides with no notes, and lists any warnings from a pandoc fallback.

## Using it from Emacs

Add a small private module, `private/swamp-present`, next to `private/swamp`:

- `SPC m p b` runs `swamp model method run <deck> build --input source=<buffer-file-name>` asynchronously. Then it reads the artifact with `swamp data query 'model("<deck>") && name == "deck-<slug>"' --select content`, writes it to a temp file and calls `browse-url`.
- `SPC m p o` runs `outline` and shows the titles and notes gaps in a side buffer.
- File-local `#+SWAMP_DECK: <instance>` sets which instance a buffer uses, defaulting to a single `talks` instance.

You keep writing in plain Org with the reveal keywords you already know. Swamp handles the builds, versioning and provenance.

## Where it lives

- **Extension source:** `presentation/` in this repo. It follows the same rules as every other extension: Apache-2.0, `license:`, `LICENSE.md`, inline `npm:zod@4.6.5`, and a quality score of 100%.
- **Instances and decks:** a separate working swamp repo, either `~/src/webframp/talks` or a `talks/` directory under `~/org`. This repo only ships extension source, not live instances.

## Open questions before building

- **Does org-re-reveal 3.39 work with reveal.js 6.x?** Doom pins reveal.js 6.0.1. org-re-reveal's layout settings target 4.x and later, and I haven't confirmed 6.x works. The first build should check the generated `<script src>` paths. If they don't work, default the CDN to 5.x and set `org-re-reveal-revealjs-version "4"`.
- **What does `--select content` return for a file artifact?** I haven't confirmed whether it gives the bytes or a path. That changes the Emacs helper slightly.
- **Does `org-re-reveal-single-file` inline reveal.js itself?** It needs a local `revealRoot` to do so. With the CDN default, a single-file deck still needs a network connection when presented.

I can write this up as a page if you want to share it or work from it.

content.text:
I need to correct something from my last message. I said nothing in your config sets `org-re-reveal-root`, so it falls back to `./reveal.js`. That's wrong. A search that was still running found Doom's own setup file, `~/.config/emacs/sources/doom+/modules/lang/org/contrib/present.el`, and it sets the root itself:

```elisp
(setq org-re-reveal-root
      (concat "file://" (expand-file-name "../../" (locate-library "dist/reveal.js" t))))
```

So your exports in Emacs today use Doom's local reveal.js 6.0.1 through a `file://` link. They work on your machine, but the HTML depends on that local path. Opened on another machine, or after a Doom upgrade moves the straight dirs, the deck loses its JavaScript and CSS.

This changes three things in the design:

- **Which reveal.js the `revealRoot` setting uses.** The `local:<path>` option should find the same checkout Doom uses (`straight/repos/reveal.js`), so a swamp build matches what `C-c C-e v v` gives you. The default stays `cdn`, pinned to a version, because a deck stored in swamp data has to work outside your machine. A `file://` link inside a stored file is exactly the portability bug above.
- **Self-contained builds have a path that should work.** Doom already gives org-re-reveal a local reveal.js, so `org-re-reveal-single-file` should be able to inline it. A single-file `build` would use the local root and the CDN only as a fallback. I haven't run this yet, so it's still unconfirmed.
- **The reveal.js version is more pressing.** Your current Emacs exports already run on reveal.js 6.0.1, so org-re-reveal 3.39 at least loads it. Whether the plugins and themes all work on 6.x is still worth testing on the first build. When `cdn` is chosen, it should pin to 6.0.1 so Emacs and swamp builds use the same version.

The rest of the design still holds. That leaves two open questions: what `--select content` returns for a file artifact, and whether single-file inlining works with the local root.

"Does org-re-reveal 3.39 work with reveal.js 6.x?" I don't know, why would you ask me that? figure it out with our own local sandboxed, safe tests. Same for the other questions, don't ask me things you can learn yourself if you actually did a modicum of work

You're right. Those were all things I could test myself. I'll run them now in the scratchpad, against your real Emacs, Doom's straight packages, pandoc and chromium, without changing any of your repos.

(defun org-re-reveal--highlight-css-path (info)
  "Return location of CSS for highlight plugin with INFO."
  (let ((highlight-css (plist-get info :reveal-highlight-css))
        (version (org-re-reveal--guess-revealjs-version info)))
    (if (symbolp highlight-css)
        (concat "%r/" (format "%s/%s.css"
                              (if (version< version "4")
                                  "lib/css"
                                (if (version< version "6")
                                    "plugin/highlight"
                                  "dist/plugin/highlight"))
                              highlight-css))
      highlight-css)))

(defun org-re-reveal--theme-path (theme css-path)
  "Return the path to the themes CSS file.
If the theme already is a path (e.g. THEME is '/css/my-theme.css', detected by
checking for the suffix '.css') then return THEME, else locate THEME within
CSS-PATH for built in themes."
  (if (string-suffix-p ".css" theme t)
      theme
    (let* ((css-path (file-name-as-directory css-path))
           (theme-path (file-name-as-directory (concat css-path "theme")))
           (theme-css (concat theme-path theme ".css")))
      theme-css)))

(unless (fboundp 'mapcan)
  (defun mapcan (func sequence)
    "Apply FUNC to each element of SEQUENCE.
Concatenate the results by altering them (using `nconc')."
  (apply #'nconc (mapcar func sequence))))

(defun org-re-reveal-stylesheets (info)
  "Return HTML code for reveal stylesheets using INFO and `org-re-reveal-root'."
  (let* ((root-path (file-name-as-directory (plist-get info :reveal-root)))
         (reveal-version (org-re-reveal--guess-revealjs-version info))
         (css-path (file-name-as-directory
                    (concat root-path (plist-get info :reveal-css-path))))
         (reveal-css (concat css-path "reveal.css"))
         (theme (plist-get info :reveal-theme))
         (theme-css (org-re-reveal--theme-path theme css-path))
         (extra-css (plist-get info :reveal-extra-css))
         (enabled-plugins (org-re-reveal--enabled-plugins info))
         (plugin-css (mapcan
                      (lambda (plugin)
                        (nthcdr 3 (org-re-reveal--plugin-config plugin info)))
                      enabled-plugins))
         (in-single-file (if (plist-get info :reveal-single-file)
                             'must
                           (plist-get info :reveal-embed-local-resources))))
    (concat
     ;; Default embedded style sheets
     "<style type=\"text/css\">
.underline { text-decoration: underline; }
</style>
"
     ;; stylesheets
     (mapconcat (lambda (elem) (org-re-reveal--css-label
                                in-single-file (car elem) (cdr elem)))
                (append (list (cons reveal-css nil)
                              (cons theme-css "theme"))
                        (mapcar (lambda (path) (cons path nil))
                                (cl-delete-duplicates
                                 (mapcar (lambda (path)
                                           (replace-regexp-in-string
                                            "^%s" root-path path))
                                         (split-string extra-css "\n" t))
                                 :test #'equal))
                        (mapcar (lambda (path)
                                  (cons (org-re-reveal--reveal-path
                                         path root-path)
                                        nil))
                                plugin-css))
                "\n")

     ;; Include CSS for highlight.js if necessary
     (if (org-re-reveal--using-highlight.js info)
         (format "<link rel=\"stylesheet\" href=\"%s\"/>\n"
                 (format-spec (org-re-reveal--highlight-css-path info)
                              `((?r . ,(directory-file-name root-path)))))
       "")

     ;; Include CSS for klipse if necessary
     (org-re-reveal--klipsify-header info)

     ;; print-pdf
     (if (or in-single-file
             (version< "3.9" reveal-version))
         ""
       (format "\n<!-- If the query includes 'print-pdf', include the PDF print sheet -->
<script>
    if( window.location.search.match( /print-pdf/gi ) ) {
        var link = document.createElement( 'link' );
        link.rel = 'stylesheet';
        link.type = 'text/css';
        link.href = '%scss/print/pdf.css';
        document.getElementsByTagName( 'head' )[0].appendChild( link );
    }

content.text:
I answered every open question by testing it myself in the scratchpad, against your real Emacs 31.1, Doom's straight packages, pandoc 3.7 and chromium. Your repos and dotfiles weren't touched. To check each deck I rendered it in headless chromium and read back reveal's live state: ready, slide count, plugins, highlighting, fragments and images.

## What I found

**Org through org-re-reveal 3.39 on reveal.js 6.0.1: works.**
- 3.39 supports reveal.js 6 directly and emits the 6.x paths (`dist/plugin/<name>.js`).
- With a local root it detects the version by checking for those files. With a CDN root it can't, and the export aborts unless `org-re-reveal-revealjs-version` is set to `"6"`. With that set, the CDN build passes too.
- A `emacs --batch -Q` build that loads only org, htmlize and org-re-reveal takes about 1 second and produces the same deck as Doom.

**Single-file builds need one fix in the build script.**
- `org-re-reveal-single-file` inlines reveal.js, every plugin, the theme and images (1.8 MB). But 3.39 always writes the highlight CSS as a `<link>` to a `file://` path, because that line bypasses the single-file code.
- On another machine the deck still runs, but code blocks lose their highlighting colors.
- A small rewrite of the generated stylesheet output in the build script inlines that CSS. The patched deck then renders fully offline from another directory, highlighting included.

**Pandoc does not work with reveal.js 6 out of the box.**
- Its template uses the 5.x plugin paths, so Reveal fails with `RevealNotes is not defined`. Its default URL is also a floating `unpkg.com/reveal.js@^5`, not a pinned version.
- Rewriting the plugin paths in the template fixes it. Two more settings are needed: `--slide-level=2`, because pandoc guessed 1 and flattened the vertical slides, and `--embed-resources` for a single file. With those, the Markdown deck matches org-re-reveal, works offline, and rebuilds byte-identically.

**Pandoc's Org reader is a poor fallback.**
- `#+BEGIN_NOTES` comes out as `<div class="NOTES">`, which reveal.js doesn't treat as notes, so your speaker notes show on the slide.
- It also drops `#+ATTR_REVEAL` fragments and `#+REVEAL_THEME`.

**Browser-side markdown (reveal's own markdown plugin, no build tools) works on 6.0.1** with notes, fragments, highlighting and images.

**Reading a deck back out of swamp works.**
- A throwaway model in a scratch swamp repo ran Emacs from inside the model and stored a `text/html` file artifact.
- `swamp data query '<pred>' --select content` returns the exact bytes plus one trailing newline. They match the stored file at `.swamp/data/<type>/<id>/<name>/<v>/raw`. The `--json` output leaves `content` and `path` empty, so the Emacs helper must use `--select content`.
- The stored deck renders offline.

**Swamp issues I hit:**
- A file and a resource can't share a data name in one run.
- The run that failed on that clash had already saved both writes, so validation happens after the writes. The `deck-talk` name now has an HTML file as v1 of a JSON resource's history.

**Rebuilds:**
- Pandoc output is byte-identical every time.
- org-re-reveal changes on every run: timestamps (removed with `org-export-time-stamp-file nil`) and random heading IDs (`org9b110b9`). Setting `org-re-reveal-generate-custom-ids` doesn't help when `num:nil` is set. A fixed seed, `(random "swamp-deck")`, does make the output identical.

**PDF:**
- Chromium's `--print-to-pdf` with `?print-pdf` gives one blank page, because it prints before reveal finishes laying out the print pages.
- A 30-line Node script that drives chromium through its debugging protocol waits for the layout and then prints. It produced an 8-page PDF with the right text (title, slides, fragment steps 5.1/5.2) and needs no npm packages.

## Changes to the design

1. Pin reveal.js 6.0.1, the version Doom uses, in one constant. The `cdn` mode always passes `revealjs-version "6"`.
2. The Emacs build script sets the fixed seed, turns off the export timestamps, and inlines the leftover highlight CSS.
3. Pandoc builds ship a reveal.js 6 template inside the extension and always pass `--slide-level=2`.
4. Org always builds through org-re-reveal. If Emacs isn't available, `build` fails with a clear error instead of producing a deck with notes showing on the slides.
5. Data names: the resource is `deck-<slug>`, the HTML file `deck-<slug>-html`, the PDF `deck-<slug>-pdf`. Keeping them distinct also avoids the version-history problem above.
6. Repeat builds are byte-identical, so `build` can skip when the output hash matches the latest version, not only when the source hash does.
7. `export_pdf` uses the DevTools-protocol approach, not `--print-to-pdf`.
8. The Emacs helper reads the deck with `--select content` and drops the trailing newline.

Everything I made is in the scratchpad: the decks, `build.el` with the fixes, the `rv6.tpl` template, `pdf.mjs`, and the scratch swamp repo. I didn't file the swamp validation issue; I can if you want, since it's a public post.

## Expected

Either all of a method execution's outputs commit, or none of them do. A method
that fails should leave the model's recorded state as it was.

## Why this is worse than a partial write

The surviving artifact carries no trace of the failed run. Its full record
is indistinguishable from one written by a method that completed:

    {
      "name": "a",
      "version": 1,
      "tags": { "type": "resource", "specName": "first", "modelName": "atom3" },
      "ownerDefinition": { "ownerType": "model-method", "ownerRef": "a27ee7ab-…" },
      "createdAt": "2026-07-27T15:38:13.793Z"
    }

There is no run-outcome field anywhere on it. @swamp/method-summary does
record {"status": "failed", "method": "partial"}, so the failure is not lost —
but it lives in a separate report, and correlating an artifact with it means
matching by definition and timestamp.

A downstream workflow step reading data.latest("atom3", "a") gets the
half-written value and has no way to know. So the failure is silent at exactly
the layer that consumes the data.

## Why I hit it

I am building lab instrument drivers as swamp model types — currently a plate
reader over its USB-FTDI bridge.

Instruments produce many readings per operation, and since the write lock scopes
to the model definition (two method run invocations against one definition
serialise), the sensible shape is a single method that emits many outputs rather
than many method runs. A 96-well read is one execution writing 96 resources.

That method failing at well 60 is this bug: 59 readings persist, nothing marks
them as partial, and the next step reading data.latest() cannot tell. The more
faithfully I follow the pattern the lock pushes me toward, the more outputs each
failure can strand.

#1451 Add rollbackOnFailure for method-level write atomicity
Type: feature  Status: shipped  Author: stack72
Assignees: stack72
Comments: 0

## Summary

Add an opt-in rollbackOnFailure flag on method definitions that provides all-or-nothing write semantics. When a method declares rollbackOnFailure: true, its writes use a deferred-latest mode: data persists to disk immediately but the latest marker is not advanced. On success, markers advance. On failure, version directories are deleted. No TOCTOU window.

This is the direct fix for #1430 — the method-level complement to the workflow-level guard (#1437, shipped in #1993) and resume --from (#1444).

## Motivation

writeResource() commits per-call. A method that writes 96 resources and fails at resource 60 leaves 59 resources persisted as latest with no trace of the failed execution. For batch operations (instrument readings, bulk data transforms, multi-resource provisioning), the incomplete set looks complete to any consumer reading data.latest().

The workflow layer now handles this via guards — downstream steps won't consume partial data. But the data layer still has the problem for standalone method run and for any direct data.latest() consumer outside a workflow context.

## Design

### The rollbackOnFailure flag

An optional boolean on MethodDefinition. Defaults to false (current behavior unchanged).

    methods: {
      readAll: {
        description: "Read all 96 wells",
        rollbackOnFailure: true,
        arguments: z.object({}),
        execute: async (args, ctx) => {
          for (const well of wells) {
            const reading = await instrument.read(well);
            await ctx.writeResource("reading", well, reading);
          }
          await ctx.writeResource("scan", "complete", { wellCount: 96 });
          return {};
        },
      },
    }

### Deferred-latest write mode

When rollbackOnFailure: true:

    1. **During execution**: `writeResource()` persists the version directory and content to disk but **skips the `latest` marker update** and the catalog `is_latest` flag. Read-after-write within the method returns the previous version — the method author has the data in variables already.
    2. **On success**: Advance all `latest` markers for the collected handles. Data becomes visible to `data.latest()`.
    3. **On failure**: Delete the version directories for all collected handles. Safe — `latest` markers were never advanced, no concurrent reader saw the data. No TOCTOU window.

### Why deferred-latest, not rollback-after-write

We considered advancing markers during writes and rolling back on failure (delete + restore markers). This has a TOCTOU window: between the first write and the rollback completion, concurrent readers can see data that will be deleted. Deferred-latest eliminates this entirely — markers are never advanced, so there's nothing to roll back.

### Two completely independent write paths

CRITICAL: The default path (rollbackOnFailure not set) must be completely unchanged:

    * `writeResource()` persists to disk AND updates the `latest` marker immediately
    * `readResource()` sees the write via the marker
    * On failure, writes persist (current behavior)
    * Zero behavioral change for existing methods

The fork point is in createResourceWriter — check the flag, choose the write mode. The two paths share no mutable state.

### Implementation approach

    * Add a `saveDeferred()` method to `UnifiedDataRepository` (separate from `save()`, not a flag — prevents accidental misuse in the default path)
    * `createResourceWriter` checks the `rollbackOnFailure` flag and calls `saveDeferred()` instead of `save()` when set
    * Same treatment for `createFileWriterFactory`
    * `InProcessExecutor` on success: call a new `advanceLatestMarkers()` for collected handles
    * `InProcessExecutor` on failure: call `repo.delete(type, modelId, name, version)` for each handle
    * `DefaultMethodExecutionService`: thread the `rollbackOnFailure` flag through to the executor
    * Marker advancement on success should handle partial failure gracefully — log and continue if one marker fails to advance

### Remote worker path

The deferred-latest mode must apply on the orchestrator's data plane when the method declares rollbackOnFailure. The worker's HTTP write requests need a flag indicating the write mode so the orchestrator skips the latest marker on its end.

### The method author's contract

rollbackOnFailure: true means:

    * "My writes are a batch — commit them all on success, discard them all on failure"
    * "I don't need to read back my own writes during execution — I have the data in variables"
    * "Partial writes from my method are garbage, not a partial view of reality"

Methods that interact with external systems and write data reflecting real-world state should NOT set this flag — their writes may be the most accurate picture of reality even if the method failed.

## Files affected

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /home/sme/.claude/skills/writing-editorial

# Editorial Principles

Two layers govern every revision. **Benjamin Dreyer** supplies correctness: the
grammar that keeps a sentence from saying something it does not mean. **Verlyn
Klinkenborg** (*Several Short Sentences About Writing*) supplies the sentence:
its sound, its economy, and the discipline of knowing exactly what it says.

The governing test, from Klinkenborg, applies to every sentence:

> Know what each sentence says, what it doesn't say, and what it implies. Of
> these, the hardest is knowing what each sentence actually says.

**Economy comes first.** When any rule below would produce a longer sentence
that carries no more meaning, the rule does not apply. Revise toward removing
words, not adding them.

## 1. Dreyer: The Correctness Layer

Correct grammar is the precondition for being sure a sentence says what you
think it says. Learn the rules so they never obtrude on a reader because you
ignored them.

### 1.1. Parallelism Within a List

When a list of three or more elements is introduced by an infinitive (`to` +
verb) or joined by a coordinating conjunction, every element shares the same
grammatical form.

* **Error:** `to **strengthen**, **encourage**, **solidifying**, and
  **fostering**`
* **Correction:** find the governing structure (here, the infinitive `to`) and
  convert every item to match: `to **strengthen**, **encourage**,
  **solidify**, and **foster**`.

This rule governs the inside of a list. It does not license parallel patterns
across sentences; see 3.4.

### 1.2. Choose the Form by the List's Function

Before fixing a list's form, identify its job in the sentence:

* If the list names **activities, qualities, or concepts** (functioning as a
  noun or adjective), use **gerunds/participles**: "*Encouraging*
  collaboration is difficult."
* If the list states **actions, commands, or purposes** (functioning as a verb
  or part of an infinitive), use **base verbs**: "We must *encourage*
  collaboration."

When a series states goals or actions, default to the base verb. It is more
direct and more economical.

### 1.3. Grammar That Causes Ambiguity

These errors create a second, wrong reading. Fix every one:

* **Dangling opening modifiers.** A modifying phrase at the start of a sentence
  must modify the subject. "After seven hours of zooming and twisting through
  the air, the day had come to its end" says the day was flying.
* **Pronouns with the wrong antecedent.** A pronoun points to the nearest
  plausible noun, whatever you intended. Check every `it`, `this`, `which`,
  and `they`.
* **Misplaced phrases.** Put every phrase next to what it modifies. "Displayed
  in glass cases and lit up like jewelry, tuna is cherished in Japan" reads
  better with the tuna first.
* **Shifted person or tense.** A sudden "you" in a first-person passage, or
  layered past tenses ("had started planning... since"), confuses the reader.
  Prefer the simple past and give clear time cues.
* **Wrong words.** "Culminated into," "distinguishable" for "distinctive,"
  "random" for "unfamiliar." Look up even familiar words when you have a
  doubt, and especially when you don't.

## 2. Klinkenborg: The Sentence Layer

### 2.1. Write for Both Readers

Every reader is two readers at once. One reads with overwhelming literalness:
if a sentence offers two paths, this reader takes the wrong one, and stumbles
over every misspelling and syntactic miscue. The other is intelligent,
curious, and will follow you anywhere as long as the prose is clear. Write for
both together. The literal reader catches ambiguity; the trusting reader frees
you from over-explaining.

### 2.2. Listen

The ear catches what the eye misses, because the eye cannot see rhythm or hear
unwanted repetition. Read the text aloud, plainly, and stop wherever something
sounds off.

That faint unease, a "small internal quaver," is the most useful evidence you
will get. You may not be able to name its cause at first. Find it anyway. The
cause may be ambiguity, awkward syntax, a weak verb, or the sentence's relation
to some *other* sentence, not the sentence itself.

### 2.3. Vary Length and Structure

"Variation is the life of prose, in length and in structure." Look for
sameness and work against it. You would not repeat the same word over and over,
so do not repeat the same sentence shape. Repetition is acceptable only when
the reader can feel the reason for it, and even then it should be less parallel
than it could be.

**Self-check:** put each sentence on its own line. Look at the column. Do the
lengths vary? How many sentences open the same way (with the subject, with
"When/Since/While/Because," with "There" or "It")? How many share the same
skeleton?

### 2.4. Short Sentences, Not Choppy Ones

Short sentences restore the directness of subject and verb and make ambiguity
easier to see. "Only a string of choppy sentences sounds choppy." The common
failure is the opposite: the overcrowded sentence, huddling related ideas
together because the writer fears the reader will get lost at a period. Most
overcrowded sentences break apart easily. Long sentences are welcome when they
are as clear and direct as short ones; a strong long sentence is strong short
sentences joined.

Most sentences need no preamble. Keep the space between the period and the
next subject empty.

### 2.5. Subjects That Act, Verbs That Fit

* **The subject should be an actor capable of the verb.** "Bread, rice, and
  bananas constituted my diet" becomes "I ate mostly bread, rice, and
  bananas." Passive constructions hide the actor and absolve everyone of
  responsibility; use them only when the actor truly does not matter.
* **Never substitute noun phrases for verbs.** "The watching of," "an
  appreciation of," "the realization that," "made a decision to" all drain
  energy from a sentence. Turn them back into verbs.
* **Prefer energetic verbs to ones that merely connect, arrange, present, or
  relate.** Watch "to be" verbs, "constitute," "reside," "serve as."
  "Is" is fine when it is the plain, honest verb; do not dodge it with
  "resides."
* **The verb must fit its subject literally.** Rinds don't squat; steeples
  don't sit; a school doesn't reside. In technical prose, "the function
  returns" fits. "The schema knows" does not; see 3.10.

### 2.6. Names and Metaphor

* **Use the names of things.** Category words hide the specific: "colorful
  flora," "an array of," "the architecture" (for the buildings). In technical
  prose, name the actual service, command, flag, or file.
* **A metaphor must be literally accurate,** and the less you use one, the
  stronger it is. Do not extend a metaphor across several sentences. Do not
  let a literal noun perform a metaphorical action mid-sentence.

### 2.7. Diagnostic Questions

Run these against a draft, sentence by sentence:

* Does the sentence open with "There is" or "It was"? ("There is an old man
  who lives there" becomes "An old man lives there.")
* Does an opening "While," "Since," or "Because" steer the reader before the
  sentence starts? ("Since" also carries an unwanted overtone of "because.")
* Are the nouns abstractions ending in "-ion," or the names of actual things?
* How far is the subject from its verb? Does an inserted phrase stall it?
* Is "as" forcing a false simultaneity? It is nearly always trouble; "and," a
  period, or nothing usually works better.
* Is "with" posing as a conjunction or relative pronoun? It can only be a
  preposition. ("Los Angeles is the largest city in California with a
  population of over four million" is about a set of cities.)
* Is "due to" or "from... to" doing work a verb or a plain list should do?
* Are there empty frequency or category adjectives ("occasional," "random,"
  "typical")? "Occasional cars flash past" becomes "Cars flash past now and
  then."
* Is an adverb redundant with its verb ("wobbled uncertainly")?
* Does the sentence make explicit what is already implicit ("the awning of
  branches that hung over us")?
* Is there false specificity ("decreasing exponentially") or false logic?
* Can the sentence do without "the"? Try removing it.
* Are words repeated unintentionally?
* Does a sentence promise something the next one fails to deliver? "If there is
  one landmark here, it is not..." promises the landmark.
* Can the sentence be broken in two or three?
* Can you imagine saying it aloud? Adjust it until you can.

### 2.8. How to Revise

* **The simplest revision is deletion.** Every word is optional until it proves
  essential. Remove words one by one and listen for what is lost or gained.
* **Reimagine; do not shuffle.** "You can almost never fix a sentence by using
  only the words it already contains." If they were the right words, the
  sentence would not need fixing. The same holds for paragraphs.
* **Ask, "What exactly am I trying to say?"** The answer is often the sentence
  to write down.
* **Revise toward** brevity (remove words), directness (nothing evasive or
  periphrastic), simplicity (in construction and word choice), clarity (watch
  for ambiguity), rhythm (where it is lacking), literalness (as an antidote to
  obscurity), implication (the sentence's silent utterance), variation
  (always), silence (leave some), the names of things, and presence (the quiet
  authority of the prose).

## 3. Anti-Patterns

Each pattern below violates a principle above. Avoid them while drafting and
flag them in review. When a fix would add words without adding meaning, the
economy rule wins.

### 3.1. Defending Against Criticism the Reader Has Not Made

"This is not a gimmick." If it is not, proceed. Preempting objections that do
not exist distrusts the reader (2.1).

### 3.2. Aphoristic Summaries and Restated Conclusions

Do not follow a concrete explanation with a one-line restatement; the concrete
version is always stronger. The same applies at the scale of a piece: do not
save the point for the end, and do not end by restating it. Lead with the
point. This matters most in PR/MR descriptions and reports.

### 3.3. Template Phrases Repeated Across Items

State a structural pattern once or twice, then trust the reader to carry it.
Three or four repetitions of "The same pattern you would use to..." read as
generated, not authored (2.3).

### 3.4. Parallel Patterns Across Sentences

Parallelism and contrast patterns that cast themselves forward into later
sentences "seem to offer structure and guidance, but they're tying your hands."
They also force weak verbs: "Mornings are had in loneliness, and evenings are
had in relief" sacrifices its verb to keep the parallel. When a sentence feels
obliged to take a predetermined shape, question the obligation.

### 3.5. Announcing Structure, Transitional Sentences, Throat-Clearing

"No sentence can afford to be merely transitional." Topic sentences and
journalistic nut grafs exist only to announce what comes next. "This is X
applied to Y:" or "The X metaphor has a natural endpoint" label a structure
instead of showing it. Openings that generalize before starting are the same
fault: begin the piece, do not introduce it. If the prose is clear, the reader
will not get lost between sentences.

### 3.6. Logical Indicators

*In fact, Indeed, Moreover, However, Therefore, Thus, Of course, On the one
hand, On the other hand, Whereas.* These words "insist upon logic whether it
exists or not." They usually come first, steering the reader from the front as
if the reader could not follow a turn mid-sentence. If the order is sound, it
needs no indicators; it will be obvious when one sentence negates or affirms
another.

* Remove "but" where you can and check whether the reversal still reads.
* Prefer "but" to "however," except where rhythm, formality, or context argue
  otherwise. A sentence may begin with "But" (or "And").

### 3.7. Intensifiers and Hyperbole

"Truly," "sacred," "utmost," "incredibly," "deeply." A sentence that insists
"dies by overemphasis." Let it relax and trust the reader to take the point.
Hyperbole used for humor almost never succeeds.

### 3.8. Stacked Short Declaratives That Restate One Point

"X did not do this. Y did not do that. Z produced it." Short sentences are
fine; restatement and identical shape are the fault. The three-beat staccato of
interchangeable sentences is the most recognizable AI cadence in technical
prose.

* **Test:** does each sentence say its own piece and leave the stage, or do
  they repeat one point with slight variation?
* **Fix:** cut the sentences that restate. Vary the shape of the ones that
  remain. Combine into one sentence only when the result is no longer and no
  more crowded (2.4).
* Short declaratives that each carry one complete idea, where the last breaks
  the rhythm or pivots the argument, earn their brevity.

### 3.9. Volunteer Sentences and Cliches

Some sentences "volunteer a shape of their own and supply their own words."
They are nearly always unacceptable: predictable in structure, built from
phrases that cluster together "naturally." A cliche is "the debris of someone
else's thinking," and irony or quotation marks do not rescue it. Generated
prose is especially prone to volunteer sentences. Treat any phrase that arrived
without a decision as a candidate for replacement.

### 3.10. Anthropomorphizing Code Artifacts

Models, functions, and schemas do not "know," "understand," "want," or
"care." Say what they are or what they do. This is a case of 2.5: the verb must
fit its subject literally.

## 4. House Style

These rules come from the user, not from Dreyer or Klinkenborg. Apply them
anyway:

* No "It is not X. It is Y." constructions, singly or repeated.
* No stacked declaratives restating one point, especially in closings (see
  3.8).

content.text:
I filed the bug as [swamp-club #3700](https://swamp-club.com/lab/3700). The report says the default write path saves both outputs before rejecting the duplicate name, leaving one name with a file version and a resource version. It also says `rollbackOnFailure: true` already handles this correctly, and points to #1430 and #1451 so it isn't mistaken for the partial-write behavior those issues document as intended. I checked the posted version and it matches what I wrote.

## A reusable package

The prototype only works on your machine because it uses Doom's local copies of org-re-reveal and reveal.js. Making it reusable mostly means deciding where those dependencies come from for someone without Doom.

**Pieces:**

| Piece | What it is |
|---|---|
| `@webframp/presentation` | One model type, `deck`, with `build`, `outline` and `export_pdf`, plus the `presentation-build` workflow and the `deck-summary` report. |
| Build scripts | The Emacs build script (fixed seed, no timestamps, highlight-CSS inlining), the pandoc template for reveal.js 6, and the PDF export script. |
| Emacs side | Build, preview and outline commands that call the model. |

**Where the build scripts live.** No extension in this repo reads bundled non-code files at runtime; `additionalFiles` only carries README and LICENSE. So the build script, the pandoc template and the PDF code would be TypeScript string constants that get written to a temp directory per build, which avoids relying on an untested file-lookup path. The PDF exporter would run in Deno itself, which has a built-in WebSocket, so the Node script goes away.

**Where reveal.js comes from:**
- **Recommended:** fetch the pinned version from the npm registry once and check it against npm's published integrity hash. After that it's cached and offline. Anyone can use it, and single-file builds always have a local copy to inline.
- **Bundle it:** 5.1 MB of MIT-licensed code inside an Apache-2.0 extension. It needs a third-party license notice, and reading bundled files at runtime is untested here.
- **Point at a local copy:** for you, Doom's straight repo is found automatically. Everyone else would need their own copy.

**Where org-re-reveal comes from.** It's GPL, so I wouldn't put its source inside an Apache-2.0 extension. The options:
- **Recommended:** use `orgLoadPath` if set, otherwise find Doom or straight builds automatically, otherwise fail with a clear message. Users bring their own Emacs setup, which they need anyway to write Org decks.
- **Fetch it:** download a pinned org-re-reveal tag from GitLab into the cache, the same way as reveal.js. This works without a configured Emacs, but it's more to maintain, and the bundled Org version may differ from what users write against.

**Instances.** One instance per talks repo, for example `talks`, with defaults as global args (reveal.js version, theme, root mode). Each deck is keyed by its slug in data names, so one instance holds many decks. Per-deck settings come from the source file's own keywords, so the model never overrides what the file says.

**Where the Emacs commands live:**
- **Recommended:** add a `swamp-present.el` to `webframp/emacs-swamp`, so it's reusable by anyone with that package.
- **Doom only:** a private module in your dotfiles, simpler but only yours.

**Rules already settled by the tests:** Org always goes through org-re-reveal, with no pandoc fallback because it would show your speaker notes on the slides. Markdown defaults to pandoc with the reveal.js 6 template, and the browser-side markdown plugin is available as an option. Each output gets its own data name (`-html`, `-pdf`).

## Questions for you

1. **Name:** `@webframp/presentation`, `@webframp/revealjs`, or `@webframp/slides`? The first leaves room for formats other than reveal.js later.
2. **reveal.js source:** fetch from npm into a cache (my recommendation), bundle it, or point at a local copy?
3. **org-re-reveal source:** find it from the user's Emacs setup (my recommendation), or fetch a pinned copy?
4. **Emacs commands:** `emacs-swamp` or your dotfiles?
5. **First version scope:** all three methods plus the workflow and report, or `build` and `outline` first with PDF next?
I like it, can this live as a swamp extension in webframp/swamp-extensions or does it need to live as it's own thing?

content.text:
Yes, the swamp side fits in `webframp/swamp-extensions`. Only the Emacs commands need to live somewhere else.

**Why it fits:**

Base directory for this skill: /home/sme/.claude/skills/swamp

# Swamp

## Core Concepts

- **Behaviors** (formerly models) — typed resource definitions exposing methods
  (create, stop, destroy, sync). `swamp behavior` is the preferred spelling;
  every `swamp model` spelling still works (see
  [references/behavior/reference.md#compatibility](references/behavior/reference.md#compatibility)).
- **Data** — versioned state snapshots produced by method runs; referenced via
  CEL expressions.
- **Workflows** — declarative DAGs chaining behavior methods with guard
  expressions for idempotent execution and assert steps for validation.
- **Vaults** — secret storage referenced by behaviors at runtime.
- **Extensions** — TypeScript packages adding behavior types, vault backends,
  datastores, reports, and webhook handlers.
- **Grants** — authorization rules for swamp serve access control.
- **Serve** — exposes the repo over the network with TLS and authentication.

## Routing Table

Route to the right guide based on what the user needs.

| User intent                                                      | Guide                                                                          |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Behaviors — create, run, edit, delete, search types              | [references/behavior/guide.md](references/behavior/guide.md)                   |
| Workflows — create, run, validate, DAG, history                  | [references/workflow/guide.md](references/workflow/guide.md)                   |
| Data — list, query, versions, GC, delete                         | [references/data/guide.md](references/data/guide.md)                           |
| Vaults — create, store/read secrets, expressions                 | [references/vault/guide.md](references/vault/guide.md)                         |
| Reports — run, configure, view, filter                           | [references/report/guide.md](references/report/guide.md)                       |
| Repository — init, upgrade, datastores, sources                  | [references/repo/guide.md](references/repo/guide.md)                           |
| Extensions — create behaviors/vaults/datastores/reports/webhooks | [references/extension/guide.md](references/extension/guide.md)                 |
| Publishing — push extensions to registry, deprecate              | [references/extension-publish/guide.md](references/extension-publish/guide.md) |
| Issues — file bugs, features, security reports                   | [references/issue/guide.md](references/issue/guide.md)                         |
| Run tracking — active runs, stale detection, diagnostics         | [references/behavior/guide.md](references/behavior/guide.md)                   |
| Architecture — which primitive to use, design trade-offs         | [references/architecture/guide.md](references/architecture/guide.md)           |
| Sharing — promote solo repo to team, datastore + vault setup     | [references/share/guide.md](references/share/guide.md)                         |
| Serve — auth, grants, access control, tokens, OAuth              | [references/serve/guide.md](references/serve/guide.md)                         |
| Troubleshooting — errors, health checks, diagnostics             | [references/troubleshooting/guide.md](references/troubleshooting/guide.md)     |

## Common Commands

```bash
# Behaviors
swamp behavior create <type> <name>            # create a behavior definition
swamp behavior run @<type> <method> <name>     # run a method on a behavior
swamp behavior get <name> --json               # inspect current behavior state
swamp behavior type search [query]             # find available behavior types
swamp behavior list                            # list all behaviors in the repo

# Data
swamp data list <name>                         # list data versions for a behavior
swamp data query '<CEL predicate>'             # query data with CEL expressions
# read one item's latest content (`swamp data get` is deprecated)
swamp data query 'behavior("<name>") && name == "<data>"' --select content

# Workflows
swamp workflow create <name>                   # create a new workflow
swamp workflow validate <name>                 # validate DAG before running
swamp workflow run <name>                      # execute a workflow
swamp workflow run <name> --input key=value    # execute with inputs
swamp workflow resume <name>                   # resume a suspended workflow
swamp workflow resume <name> --run <id>        # retry a failed run's failed steps
swamp workflow resume <name> --from <step>     # re-enter failed run at step
swamp workflow history search --json           # search run history

# Run tracking
swamp run history                              # recent runs (last 24h)
swamp run history --active                     # what's running right now?
swamp run doctor                               # diagnose stale/orphaned runs
swamp run doctor --fix                         # auto-reap stale runs

# Vaults, Reports, Extensions
swamp vault create <type> <name>               # create a vault for secrets
swamp report run <name>                        # run a report
swamp extension push manifest.yaml             # publish an extension
```

## Workflow

1. **Route** — match intent to a guide in the routing table.
2. **Load** — read the guide; load its `reference.md` if needed, deeper
   `references/` only when the guide says to.
3. **Validate** — before running any workflow: `swamp workflow validate <name>`.
   Before destructive methods (delete, stop, destroy):
   `swamp behavior get <name> --json` to confirm the target exists and is in the
   expected state. Proceed only when validation passes.
4. **Verify args** — run `swamp help <subcommand>` (e.g.
   `swamp help behavior run`) to confirm exact flags and arguments before
   executing. The output is structured JSON — the canonical CLI schema. Do not
   guess flags from memory.
5. **Execute** — run the command.
6. **On failure** — load
   [references/troubleshooting/guide.md](references/troubleshooting/guide.md)
   and diagnose before retrying or changing definitions.

## Rules

1. **Use the routing table, not memory.** Don't answer from cached knowledge
   about swamp commands — always load the current guide.
2. **Consult the architecture guide for design decisions.** Before choosing
   between primitives (behavior vs. workflow vs. extension vs. report) or
   explaining a design trade-off, load
   [references/architecture/guide.md](references/architecture/guide.md) and cite
   the design doc you relied on.
3. **Use swamp commands, don't go around them.** Query data with
   `swamp data query`, not by grepping `.swamp/` files. Interact with resources
   through behavior methods, not raw CLI tools when a behavior type already
   wraps the API — check with `swamp behavior type search`. Composing with
   `--json` output (e.g. piping through `jq`) is fine — the anti-pattern is
   bypassing swamp entirely.

# Swamp Workflow Skill

Work with swamp workflows through the CLI. All commands support `--json` for
machine-readable output.

## CRITICAL: Workflow Creation Rules

- **Never generate workflow IDs** — no `uuidgen`, `crypto.randomUUID()`, or
  manual UUIDs. Swamp assigns IDs automatically via `swamp workflow create`.
- **Never write a workflow YAML file from scratch** — always use
  `swamp workflow create <name> --json` first, then edit the scaffold at the
  returned `path`, preserving the assigned `id`.
- **Never modify the `id` field** in an existing workflow file.
- **Verify CLI syntax**: Always run `swamp help workflow` to confirm exact flags
  before executing — the output is structured JSON.

Correct flow: `swamp workflow create <name> --json` → edit the YAML → validate →
run.

## Skill boundary

This skill produces a durable swamp workflow YAML under `workflows/` via
`swamp workflow create`. It is unrelated to the Claude Code Workflow tool /
dynamic workflows, to agent task lists (`TaskCreate`), to worktrees

manifestVersion: 1
name: "@webframp/extension-maintenance"
license: Apache-2.0
version: "2026.10.14.1"
description: |
  Extension repository maintenance model. Observes a multi-extension repo,
  audits dependency freshness (npm, swamp-testing, manifest pins), computes
  quality scores, plans version bumps, and applies changes with human
  approval.

  Designed for repos publishing many swamp extensions via CI. Replaces
  the manual audit → bump → test → PR loop with typed, observable methods.

  ## Usage

  ```bash
  swamp extension pull @webframp/extension-maintenance
  swamp model create @webframp/extension-maintenance/maintainer ext-maint \
    --global-arg repo_root=/path/to/extensions

  # Observe
  swamp model method run ext-maint audit

  # Plan (human reviews output)
  swamp model method run ext-maint plan-bump

  # Apply (writes files)
  swamp model method run ext-maint apply-bump

  # Verify
  swamp model method run ext-maint quality-gate
  ```

  Or run the whole sweep as one workflow, with the approval gate between
  plan and apply:

  ```bash
  swamp workflow run @webframp/extension-maintenance-sweep
  ```

dependency age. It reports the newest release published at least

2026-09-24 sweep pinned `@aws-sdk/*` 3.1140.0 hours after release;
`swamp extension quality` rejected it in CI across 21 extensions. A pin newer
than that version is no longer reported as stale, and unpublished or deprecated
npm versions are never picked. Manifest pins compare numerically too, so audit
never plans a downgrade.

name: "@webframp/extension-maintenance-sweep"
description: |
  Routine dependency-maintenance sweep across every extension in the repo:
  observe staleness, plan CalVer bumps, gate on human approval, apply, then
  verify with the quality gate.

  Replaces the manual four-command loop:
    swamp model method run ext-maint audit
    swamp model method run ext-maint plan-bump
    swamp model method run ext-maint apply-bump
    swamp model method run ext-maint quality-gate

  Requires an @webframp/extension-maintenance/maintainer instance named
  `ext-maint`, with repo_root pointing at the extension repository root:

    swamp model create @webframp/extension-maintenance/maintainer ext-maint \
      --global-arg repo_root=/path/to/swamp-extensions

  Every step targets that one model, so the steps run strictly sequentially.
  Parallelising them would contend on the per-model lock and time out.

  Rejecting the approval gate marks the run failed and leaves `apply` and
  `verify` unscheduled. That is intentional: the audit and plan data are
  already written and inspectable, and nothing was modified. To get a quality
  snapshot without bumping anything, run the gate on its own:

    swamp model method run ext-maint quality-gate

  The audit step dominates runtime — roughly five minutes across 137
  extensions, since it queries npm once per deduplicated package.

id: 8596b518-de49-4c55-b9b4-6f223f88fc9a
name: "@webframp/presentation-build"
description: |
  Build one deck: outline the source, render it, and optionally print it to
  PDF. Each step runs only if the one before it succeeded, so a source that
  fails to build never reaches the PDF step.

  Requires an @webframp/presentation/deck instance, named by the `deck`
  input (default `talks`):

    swamp model create @webframp/presentation/deck talks

  The deck's data name comes from the source file name. To choose another
  name or an engine other than the default, run the methods directly:

    swamp model method run talks build --input source=talk.md \
      --input name=talk-web --input engine=reveal-markdown

  All three steps target the same model and run in order.
version: 1
tags:
  extension: "@webframp/presentation"
  category: "presentation"
reports:
  require:
    - "@swamp/workflow-summary"
inputs:
  properties:
    deck:
      type: string
      default: talks
      description: Name of the @webframp/presentation/deck instance
    source:
      type: string
      description: Path to the .org or .md source, absolute or relative to the repository
    selfContained:
      type: boolean
      default: false
      description: Inline every reveal.js file so the deck works offline
    pdf:
      type: boolean
      default: false
      description: Also print the deck to PDF with headless Chromium
  required:
    - source
jobs:
  - name: deck
    description: Outline, build and optionally print one deck
    steps:
      - name: outline
        description: Read the source without rendering it
        task:
          type: model_method
          modelIdOrName: ${{ inputs.deck }}
          methodName: outline
          inputs:
            source: ${{ inputs.source }}
      - name: build
        description: Render the deck and store its HTML
        dependsOn:
          - step: outline
            condition:
              type: succeeded
        task:
          type: model_method
          modelIdOrName: ${{ inputs.deck }}
          methodName: build
          inputs:
            source: ${{ inputs.source }}
            selfContained: ${{ inputs.selfContained }}
      - name: pdf
        description: Print the build to PDF (skipped unless pdf is true)
        dependsOn:
          - step: build
            condition:
              type: succeeded
        guard: ${{ !inputs.pdf }}
        task:
          type: model_method
          modelIdOrName: ${{ inputs.deck }}
          methodName: export_pdf
          inputs:
            source: ${{ inputs.source }}
EOF

# @webframp/extension-maintenance

Extension repository maintenance model for swamp. Observes a multi-extension
repo, audits dependency freshness, plans version bumps, and applies changes with
human approval.

Replaces the manual audit → bump → test → PR loop with typed, observable methods
that produce versioned data at each step.

## Methods

### `audit`

Pure observation. Scans all extensions in the repo, queries npm and the swamp
registry for latest versions, computes quality scores. Produces a structured
staleness report.

```bash
swamp model method run ext-maint audit
swamp model method run ext-maint audit --input filter=aws/
```

### `plan-bump`

Reads the latest audit output and produces a structured change plan: which files
to modify, what version strings change, draft release notes. No side effects.

```bash
swamp model method run ext-maint plan-bump
swamp model method run ext-maint plan-bump --input skip_testing=true
```

### `apply-bump`

Executes the latest plan. Writes version changes, updates manifests, creates
RELEASE_NOTES.md files. Supports `dry_run` mode.

```bash
# Preview what would change
swamp model method run ext-maint apply-bump --input dry_run=true

# Apply for real
swamp model method run ext-maint apply-bump
```

### `quality-gate`

Runs the full local validation suite across all (or filtered) extensions:
`deno task check`, `lint`, `fmt`, `test`, plus `swamp extension quality` and
`swamp extension fmt --check`.

```bash
swamp model method run ext-maint quality-gate
swamp model method run ext-maint quality-gate --input filter=cloudflare
swamp model method run ext-maint quality-gate --input stop_on_failure=true
```

# @webframp/presentation

Build reveal.js presentations from Org or Markdown with swamp. Each build, its
outline and its PDF are stored as versioned swamp data, so a deck can be
opened, printed or compared against an earlier version long after its source
has moved on.

## Requirements

| Engine            | Source   | Needs                                       |
| ----------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `org-re-reveal`   | Org      | Emacs 27 or later (its built-in Org is used) |
| `pandoc`          | Markdown | pandoc 3                                    |
| `reveal-markdown` | Markdown | nothing                                     |

`export_pdf` needs Chromium or Chrome. The first build downloads what it needs
and caches it; after that, building works offline.

## Setup

```bash
swamp extension pull @webframp/presentation
swamp model create @webframp/presentation/deck talks
```

Global arguments, all optional:

| Argument            | Default                               | Purpose                                                           |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `theme`             | `black`                               | Theme for decks whose source names none                           |
| `emacs`             | `emacs`                               | Emacs executable                                                  |
| `pandoc`            | `pandoc`                              | pandoc executable                                                 |
| `chromium`          | `chromium`                            | Chromium or Chrome executable, e.g. `google-chrome` on macOS paths |
| `chromiumNoSandbox` | `false`                               | Pass `--no-sandbox`; needed in some containers                    |
| `cacheDir`          | `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/webframp-presentation` | Where pinned downloads are kept (`~/.cache/...` without XDG)      |

## Methods

### `build`

Renders a source and stores the HTML.

```bash
swamp model method run talks build --input source=talk.org
swamp model method run talks build --input source=talk.md --input engine=reveal-markdown
swamp model method run talks build --input source=talk.org --input selfContained=true --input name=talk-offline
```

| Input           | Default | Meaning                                                                  |
| --------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `source`        |         | Path to the `.org` or `.md` file, absolute or relative to the repository |
| `content`       |         | Source text instead of a file; needs `name` and `format`                 |
| `format`        | `auto`  | `org`, `markdown`, or `auto` (from the extension)                        |
| `engine`        | `auto`  | `org-re-reveal` for Org, `pandoc` or `reveal-markdown` for Markdown      |
| `name`          | stem    | Deck name; defaults to the file name without its extension               |
| `selfContained` | `false` | Inline every reveal.js file so the deck works offline                    |

A rebuild whose HTML is byte-identical to the last one writes no new HTML
version. Builds are reproducible: the same source gives the same bytes.

A deck name belongs to one source. Building `slides/talk.md` after
`talk.org` fails rather than overwrite it; pass `name` to keep both.

### `outline`

Reads a source without rendering it: slide titles, words of speaker notes per
slide, the slides with none, and images that do not exist.

```bash
swamp model method run talks outline --input source=talk.org
```

### `export_pdf`

Prints the latest build with headless Chromium. If the HTML has not changed
since the last export, the existing PDF is kept.

```bash
swamp model method run talks export_pdf --input name=talk
```

A deck that loads reveal.js from the CDN needs network access to print.

## Workflow

`@webframp/presentation-build` outlines, builds and optionally prints one
deck. Each step runs only if the one before it succeeded.

```bash
swamp workflow run @webframp/presentation-build --input source=talk.org
swamp workflow run @webframp/presentation-build \
  --input deck=talks --input source=talk.org --input selfContained=true --input pdf=true
```

## Data

For a deck named `talk`:

| Data name       | Kind     | Contents                                                                          |
| --------------- | -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `deck-talk`     | resource | Engine, pinned reveal.js, theme, slides, HTML hash and version, warnings          |
| `deck-talk-html`| file     | The deck (`text/html`)                                                            |
| `outline-talk`  | resource | Slides, notes word counts, missing images                                         |
| `pdf-talk`      | resource | Page count, hashes, which HTML version was printed                                |
| `deck-talk-pdf` | file     | The PDF                                                                           |

Every method also writes a `@webframp/presentation/deck-summary` report.

```bash
# The deck, ready to open:
swamp data query 'model("talks") && name == "deck-talk-html"' --select content > talk.html
# The build record as JSON:
swamp data query 'model("talks") && name == "deck-talk"' --select content --json
```

`--select content` prints a file's bytes followed by one newline. For a
resource, add `--json`; without it the record prints as a table.

## Engines

**org-re-reveal** exports Org exactly as `C-c C-e v v` does in Emacs, with
org-re-reveal 3.39.0. `#+REVEAL_THEME`, `#+REVEAL_PLUGINS`, `#+ATTR_REVEAL`
fragments, `#+BEGIN_NOTES` and `:reveal_background:` all apply. Emacs runs with
`-Q`, so nothing in your configuration changes the result. Three settings
differ from an interactive export:

- Code blocks never run (`org-export-use-babel` is off) and file-local
  variables are ignored. Building a deck you did not write is safe.
- A deck without `#+AUTHOR` has no author. Batch Emacs would otherwise fill
  it from your login and hostname.
- There is no export timestamp, and Org's heading IDs come from a fixed seed,
  so rebuilds are byte-identical.

Org sources always use this engine. pandoc's Org reader drops `#+REVEAL_`
options and fragments, and turns speaker notes into visible slide text.

**pandoc** renders Markdown with `--slide-level=2`: level-1 and level-2
headings start slides, and level-2 headings under a level-1 heading form a
vertical stack. Speaker notes go in `::: notes` blocks. The extension takes
pandoc's own reveal.js template from `pandoc -D revealjs` and moves its plugin
paths to reveal.js 6's layout. A `theme:` in the front matter wins over the
`theme` global argument.

**reveal-markdown** wraps the Markdown in a page that reveal.js's markdown
plugin renders in the browser. A line of `---` between blank lines starts a
slide, `--` a vertical one, and text after `Note:` is speaker notes.

## reveal.js and pinned downloads

Every deck is built against reveal.js 6.0.1. Without `selfContained`, the page
loads it from `cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/reveal.js@6.0.1` and each script and
stylesheet carries an `integrity` hash, so a browser refuses a changed file.
With `selfContained`, every reveal.js file is inlined (about 1.8 MB) and the
deck opens offline. Either way, local images, videos and stylesheets are
inlined as data URIs.

Each file the extension downloads is checked against a SHA-256 in
`extensions/models/presentation/_lib/pins.ts`:

- reveal.js runtime files, from jsDelivr
- org-re-reveal 3.39.0 and htmlize 1.59, by commit URL

A download that does not match is refused, and a cached copy that no longer
matches is downloaded again. The build record's `external` field lists
anything the deck still loads from elsewhere; with `selfContained`, each entry
is also a warning. The math plugin loads KaTeX or MathJax when the deck opens,
so a deck that uses it is never fully offline.

### Moving to a new reveal.js release

1. Set `REVEAL_VERSION` in `pins.ts`.
2. Regenerate `REVEAL_FILES` from that release's npm tarball, after checking
   the tarball against the registry's `dist.integrity`:

   ```bash
   v=6.0.1
   curl -sL "https://registry.npmjs.org/reveal.js/-/reveal.js-$v.tgz" | tar xz
   (cd package && find dist -type f \( -name '*.js' -o -name '*.css' \) ! -name '*.d.ts' | sort |
     while read -r f; do printf '  "%s": "%s",\n' "$f" "$(openssl dgst -sha256 -binary "$f" | base64)"; done)
   ```

3. Run the integration tests, which download every pinned file.

## Emacs

[emacs-swamp](https://github.com/webframp/emacs-swamp) includes
`swamp-present`, which builds, previews and outlines the deck in the current
buffer through this extension. The two are independent: the extension reads no
Emacs configuration, and `swamp-present` only runs swamp commands.

## Development

```bash
deno task check && deno task lint && deno task fmt:check && deno task test
```

The integration tests run real Emacs, pandoc and Chromium and download every
pinned file:

```bash
PRESENTATION_INTEGRATION=1 deno task test
# Where Chromium's sandbox is unavailable:
PRESENTATION_INTEGRATION=1 PRESENTATION_NO_SANDBOX=1 deno task test
```

## License

Apache-2.0. reveal.js (MIT), org-re-reveal and htmlize (GPL-3.0-or-later) are
downloaded at build time and are not part of this package.

;;; ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
;;; State
;;; ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

(defvar swamp--last-result-buffer nil
  "Most recently displayed swamp result buffer.")

;;; ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
;;; Low-level helpers
;;; ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

(defun swamp--base-args ()
  "Return the base argument list (--repo-dir if configured)."
  (if swamp-repo-dir
      (list "--repo-dir" (expand-file-name swamp-repo-dir))
    nil))

(defun swamp--run-json (args)
  "Run swamp with ARGS and --json, return parsed JSON or nil on error.
ARGS is a list of strings.  The exit code determines success; JSON parse
errors are swallowed and return nil."
  (with-temp-buffer
    (let* ((full-args (append (swamp--base-args) args (list "--json")))
           (exit (apply #'call-process swamp-executable nil t nil full-args)))
      (when (= exit 0)
        (goto-char (point-min))
        (condition-case nil
            (json-parse-buffer :object-type 'alist :array-type 'list)
          (error nil))))))

(defun swamp--run-json-stream (args)
  "Run swamp with ARGS and --json, return a list of all parsed JSON objects.
Some swamp commands emit multiple newline-delimited JSON objects.
Returns a list (possibly empty) of parsed objects; never signals on parse errors."
  (with-temp-buffer
    (let ((full-args (append (swamp--base-args) args (list "--json"))))
      (apply #'call-process swamp-executable nil t nil full-args))
    (goto-char (point-min))
    (let (objects)
      (while (not (eobp))
        (condition-case nil
            (let ((obj (json-parse-buffer :object-type 'alist :array-type 'list)))
              (push obj objects))
          (error
           (forward-line 1))))
      (nreverse objects))))

(defun swamp--completing-read-model (&optional prompt)
  "Prompt for a model name using completion from the live model list.
Uses PROMPT if provided."
  (let* ((data (swamp--run-json '("model" "search")))
         (results (alist-get 'results data))
         (names (mapcar (lambda (r) (alist-get 'name r)) results)))
    (completing-read (or prompt "Model: ") names nil t)))

(defun swamp--completing-read-workflow (&optional prompt)
  "Prompt for a workflow name using completion from the live workflow list.
Uses PROMPT if provided."
  (let* ((data (swamp--run-json '("workflow" "search")))
         (results (alist-get 'results data))
         (names (mapcar (lambda (r) (alist-get 'name r)) results)))
    (completing-read (or prompt "Workflow: ") names nil t)))

;;; ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
;;; Rendering helpers
;;; ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

(defun swamp-model-method-run ()
  "Run a method on a model, prompting for model and method name."
  (interactive)
  (let* ((name   (swamp--completing-read-model "Run method on model: "))
         (method (read-string (format "Method [%s]: " name)))
         (data   (swamp--run-json (list "model" "method" "run" name method))))
    (unless data
      (user-error "Method run returned no data for %s/%s" name method))
    (let ((err (alist-get 'error data)))
      (when err (user-error "%s" err)))
    (let ((status (alist-get 'status data "")))
      (swamp--display-detail
       (format "*swamp-run:%s/%s*" name method)
       (format "Method run: %s / %s" name method)
       (list
        (list "Model"     (alist-get 'modelName data))
        (list "Method"    (alist-get 'methodName data))
        (list "Status"    (swamp--propertize-status status))
        (list "Duration"  (let ((ms (alist-get 'duration data)))
                            (when ms (format "%dms" ms))))
        (list "Log file"  (alist-get 'logFile data))
        (list "Artifacts" (mapconcat #'identity
                                     (or (alist-get 'dataArtifacts data) '())
                                     "\n                     ")))))))

;;;###autoload
(defun swamp-model-output-get ()

;;; ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
;;; Transient menus
;;; ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

;;;###autoload (autoload 'swamp-model-dispatch "swamp" nil t)
(transient-define-prefix swamp-model-dispatch ()
  "Swamp model commands."
  [["Search & Get"
    ("s" "search"     swamp-model-search)
    ("g" "get"        swamp-model-get)
    ("o" "output get" swamp-model-output-get)]
   ["Run & Validate"
    ("r" "method run" swamp-model-method-run)
    ("v" "validate"   swamp-model-validate)]])

;;;###autoload (autoload 'swamp-workflow-dispatch "swamp" nil t)
(transient-define-prefix swamp-workflow-dispatch ()
  "Swamp workflow commands."
  [["Search & Get"
    ("s" "search"  swamp-workflow-search)
    ("g" "get"     swamp-workflow-get)]

    ("r" "run"     swamp-workflow-run)
    ("h" "history" swamp-workflow-history)]])

;;;###autoload (autoload 'swamp-extension-dispatch "swamp" nil t)
(transient-define-prefix swamp-extension-dispatch ()
  "Swamp extension commands."
  [["Registry"
    ("s" "search" swamp-extension-search)]
